name: DRV5055A1ELPGMQ1
title: DRV5055-Q1 automotive ratiometric linear Hall-effect sensor
summary: The DRV5055-Q1 is a three-pin linear Hall-effect sensor qualified to AEC-Q100 grade 0. Its analog output sits at half of VCC with no field and moves in proportion to the flux density perpendicular to the package top, with both the zero-field level and the gain scaling with VCC. It runs from a 3.3 V or a 5 V supply, and the sensitivity options span 12.5 to 100 mV/mT at 5 V, including one with negative slope. The A options raise their gain with temperature to offset the weakening of NdFeB magnets; the Z2 option holds it flat. It comes in a SOT-23 (DBZ) and a through-hole TO-92 (LPG); DRV5055A1ELPGMQ1 is the 100 mV/mT option in TO-92 on ammo pack.

circuits.title: Typical schematic
circuits.description: The sensor and a controller share one supply and ground. A ceramic capacitor across VCC and GND sits at the sensor, and OUT runs straight to an ADC input of the controller; when the ADC takes the same VCC as its reference, supply tolerance drops out of the reading.

parts.note: ceramic supply bypass, 0.01 µF or larger

circuits.title: Wire fault detection circuit
circuits.description: The sensor sits on a remote board linked to the controller by a three-wire cable. A bypass capacitor spans VCC and GND at the sensor, and a pull-up resistor from OUT to VCC sets where the output goes if a wire opens or shorts: a reading within 150 mV of either rail marks a fault. The pull-up is 20 kΩ to 100 kΩ, and its current plus any ADC input current must stay within the ±1 mA output rating.

operation.text: Inside are the Hall element with its bias, offset cancellation, temperature compensation and mechanical stress cancellation, a bandgap reference, trim registers, a precision amplifier and an output driver. The output voltage is proportional to flux density and referenced to VCC. There is one operating mode, in force whenever the recommended operating conditions hold.

Only the field component perpendicular to the package top is sensed, so the SOT-23 and the TO-92 respond to fields along different axes relative to the board. Flux entering the bottom and leaving the marked top face, as with a south pole facing the top, counts as positive B; the reverse is negative.

With no field OUT sits at VQ, about VCC / 2; north and south fields drive it in opposite directions. The response is linear while OUT lies within VL (0.2 V to VCC – 0.2 V); beyond that the gain falls off and the curve bends toward the rail. SLE compares sensitivity between any two fields of the same sign; SSE compares a positive field with the negative field of equal size.
Quiescent voltage and sensitivity both scale linearly with VCC: 5.25 V gives values 5% above those at 5 V. An ADC referenced to the same VCC therefore reads the same code across supply tolerance.

The recommended supplies are 3 V to 3.63 V and 4.5 V to 5.5 V. Between 3.63 V and 4.5 V the part keeps running, but a crossover threshold close to 4 V changes its characteristics, so sensitivity there is not well defined.

Magnet fields weaken as they warm, so the A options raise their sensitivity with temperature: at 150°C it is typically 12% above its 25°C value. The Z2 option keeps the 25°C sensitivity at 150°C. The 0.12 %/°C rate matches the average remanence drift of NdFeB; ferrite drifts about 0.20 %/°C and is compensated only in part. Lower system temperature means smaller drift error.

After VCC is applied the output needs a short start-up before it is valid. tON runs from VCC rising through 3 V to OUT settling within 5% of VQ, measured with 0 mT and OUT unloaded; the output is invalid during that interval.

Use the most sensitive option whose BL still covers the largest flux density the application sees; this gives the widest output swing. Flux density climbs steeply as a magnet gets close, so a larger magnet at a greater distance tends to give better position accuracy than a tiny one very close. Field simulation, magnet data and testing establish the flux at the sensor.

If less than 20 kHz of bandwidth is needed, a series resistor and shunt capacitor on OUT form a low-pass filter that lowers noise and improves accuracy. A capacitor connected straight to OUT with no resistor ahead of it risks an unstable output.

Pick an option that keeps OUT within VL in normal use, then add a 20 kΩ to 100 kΩ pull-up from OUT to VCC, keeping total OUT current, ADC input included, within IO. A reading within 150 mV of VCC or GND then signals an open or shorted wire.

A common arrangement slides a bar magnet past the sensor with its north-south axis along the travel, so the sensor sees the whole range from north to south and the flux changes close to linearly with position. The worked design uses VCC = 5 V, a 15 × 5 × 5 mm NdFeB magnet, 12 mm of travel and at most ±75 mT at 25°C, and picks DRV5055A3. The magnet should approach so that its field crosses the package top, not along it.
A ceramic decoupling capacitor of at least 0.01 µF goes close to the device to supply local charge with low inductance.

Fields pass with little disturbance through non-ferromagnetic materials such as plastic, aluminium and most PCBs, so the sensor can sit inside an enclosure with the magnet outside, or with the magnet on the far side of the board.
